meta.title: MCP Question Bank — Chapter 6: Client Best Practices (Progressive Discovery & Code Mode)
meta.chapterName: Client Best Practices (Progressive Discovery & Code Mode)

questions.question: What problem does progressive tool discovery solve for MCP hosts connected to many servers?

options.text: Slow network transports
Loading every tool definition into the model's context upfront wastes tokens, adds latency, and degrades model performance
Servers refusing to list their tools
OAuth token expiry

questions.explanation: With hundreds of tools, upfront definitions can consume most of the context window. Progressive discovery defers injecting definitions, exposing a lightweight search_tools meta-tool and loading full definitions only as needed.

questions.question: In the three-layer progressive discovery pattern, what are the layers?

options.text: Catalog, Inspect, Execute
Search, Sort, Send
List, Cache, Call
Discover, Authorize, Invoke

questions.explanation: Layer 1 (Catalog): a search_tools meta-tool returns matching names with brief descriptions. Layer 2 (Inspect): the model fetches the full definition of only the tool it needs. Layer 3 (Execute): the model calls the tool with full knowledge of its interface.

questions.question: What threshold do the docs recommend for switching from loading all tools to progressive discovery?

options.text: When more than 100 servers are connected
When tool definitions consume roughly 1%–5% of the context window
When any single tool schema exceeds 1 MB
Progressive discovery should always be used, regardless of size

questions.explanation: For a small tool set, loading everything is fine. Clients should implement a threshold as a percentage of the context window — for example 1%–5% — and switch to progressive discovery once tool definitions cross it.

questions.question: What is 'programmatic tool calling' (code mode)?

options.text: The model writes code that calls tools; the code runs in a sandbox and only the final result returns to the model
Tools written exclusively in Python
A mode where the server executes tools without client approval
Pre-compiling tool schemas to WebAssembly

questions.explanation: Instead of round-tripping every intermediate result through the model's context, the model writes a script against typed APIs generated from MCP tool schemas. The sandbox executes it, intermediate data flows between servers via the host broker, and only e.g. a console.log summary returns to the model.

questions.question: In a code-mode architecture, which statement about credentials and network access is correct?

options.text: The sandbox holds API keys so tool calls are faster
The sandbox should have no direct network access; credentials are held by the host broker, which adds authentication when forwarding calls to servers
The model receives all tokens so it can decide which to use
Each MCP server pushes its credentials into the sandbox at startup

questions.explanation: The sandbox is isolated: its only interface is the generated function stubs that route back to the host. The host acts as broker, holds authorization tokens, enforces per-call authorization, and never exposes credentials to model-generated code.

questions.question: How should generated code-mode wrappers handle an MCP tool response with isError: true?

options.text: Ignore it, since the transport succeeded
Convert it into a thrown exception so model-authored code can use try/catch
Retry the call automatically up to 10 times
Terminate the sandbox immediately without reporting

questions.explanation: MCP tool errors arrive as successful responses with isError: true, not transport failures. Wrappers should convert this into a thrown exception; if an uncaught error ends the script, surface it as the script's result so the model can self-correct.

questions.question: Which of these is a recommended implementation guideline for progressive discovery?

options.text: Re-fetch tools/list from the server every time a definition is needed
Cache tool definitions host-side once fetched, and re-index the search catalog when a notifications/tools/list_changed arrives
Hide the source server of each tool from the model
Only ever expose one tool at a time

questions.explanation: Guidelines include offering multiple detail levels, caching definitions host-side, refreshing the catalog on list_changed notifications, and grouping tools by server so the model can reason about related capabilities.

questions.question: Why can adding or removing tool definitions mid-conversation be costly even when it saves definition tokens?

options.text: Servers charge per tools/list call
It invalidates the provider's prompt cache (which includes the tools array), and the resulting cache miss can cost more tokens than the definitions removed
It forces the client to reconnect to every server
JSON-RPC requires renumbering all message IDs

questions.explanation: Most providers cache the prompt prefix including the tools array. To preserve caching, append newly discovered definitions after the cache breakpoint or route calls through a single stable call_tool meta-tool, and treat server disconnection as a conversation-boundary operation.

questions.question: In progressive discovery, what does the lightweight search_tools meta-tool return?

options.text: Full JSON Schemas for every tool on every server
Concise matches: tool names and one-line descriptions only
Executable code for each tool
A ranked list of servers to disconnect

questions.explanation: The catalog layer returns only names and brief descriptions (e.g., salesforce_updateRecord — 'Update fields on a Salesforce object'); the model then inspects the full definition of just the tool it needs.

questions.question: What is the main drawback of direct tool calling when chaining multiple tools together?

options.text: Tools cannot be chained at all
Every intermediate result flows through the model's context, consuming tokens and adding latency even when the model doesn't need it
It requires OAuth for every call
It only works over stdio

questions.explanation: With direct calling, each invocation is a round trip through the model. Programmatic tool calling (code mode) fixes this by letting data flow between servers inside a sandbox, with only the final summary returning to the model.

questions.question: Under dynamic server management, what can a host do instead of connecting to every configured server at startup?

options.text: Nothing; all servers must connect at startup
Keep a registry of available servers, connect to a server only when the model needs its capabilities, and disconnect servers no longer relevant to free context
Merge all servers into one process
Randomly sample three servers per conversation

questions.explanation: Progressive discovery extends to whole servers: maintain a registry with high-level descriptions, connect on demand (e.g., enable_server('salesforce')), and disconnect when done. This suits general-purpose agents where intent isn't known upfront.

questions.question: Which discovery strategies do the docs list for implementing search_tools?

options.text: Keyword-based, embedding-based, subagent-based, and hybrid approaches
Alphabetical sorting only
Random selection with retries
Manual user selection for every call

questions.explanation: Options include keyword matching (BM25/regex), vector-similarity embeddings, a small fast subagent model (e.g., Claude Haiku) selecting tools, or hybrids. Some providers (OpenAI, Anthropic) offer built-in tool search you may prefer.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A task requires reading thousands of error log entries, deduplicating them, and filing one ticket per unique error. Which approach keeps the log data out of the model's context?

options.text: Direct tool calling with the full log dump returned to the model each time

Code mode: the model writes a script that calls logging_getLogs, filters and deduplicates inside the sandbox, calls ticketing_createIssue per unique error, and returns only a one-line console.log summary
Asking the user to paste the logs manually
Increasing the model's max tokens

questions.explanation: This is the canonical code-mode example: log data and ticket creation flow between servers through the host broker without entering the model's context; only the summary line (e.g., 'Filed 7 tickets from 3,214 error logs') returns.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A user approves a code-mode script that will call ticketing_createIssue in a loop. Mid-run, the script tries to call payments_transferFunds, which the user never discussed. What does the security guidance say the host broker should do?

options.text: Allow it — approving the script grants blanket approval for all runtime calls
Evaluate each sandbox-originated call against the granted approval: script approval is not blanket approval, so a call outside the grant (like payments_transferFunds) requires its own authorization
Kill the sandbox and delete all tickets already created
Log it silently and continue

questions.explanation: Per-call authorization: the broker is still the MCP host for spec purposes. Hosts may grant categorical approval (e.g., 'allow ticketing_createIssue for this run') rather than prompting per iteration, but every call must still be evaluated against that grant — approving the script does not approve everything it might do.

questions.question: When a tool provides no outputSchema, what does the guidance recommend for typing its results in code mode?

options.text: Refuse to call the tool

Prefer a generic type (any/string) and handle unstructured output downstream; optionally use a host-brokered extract(value, ExpectedType) helper backed by a fast model for single-shot calls, validating the result before use
Guess the schema from the tool's name
Always regenerate the whole API from scratch

questions.explanation: The simple path is a generic type — the real fix is server authors providing outputSchema. An extract() helper routed through the host (never giving the sandbox network access) can coerce values via a small model, but it adds latency and can hallucinate, so validate against the expected type.

questions.question: A host has 2,000 available tools and injects every full schema into every model turn. Context use and latency become poor. Which strategy should a tester expect a scalable client to consider?

options.text: Progressive tool discovery: catalog, inspect likely candidates, then execute
Convert every tool into a resource
Disable tool descriptions
Use one OAuth token for all servers

questions.explanation: Progressive discovery keeps a lightweight catalog, retrieves detailed schemas only for likely tools, then executes. This reduces context pressure for large catalogs.

questions.question: A client caches a tool catalog. It receives notifications/tools/list_changed while the previous TTL has not expired. What behavior should the test expect?

options.text: Keep using the cache until TTL expiry
Invalidate/refresh because list_changed overrides the unexpired TTL
Ignore the notification because notifications never affect caches
Restart the server

questions.explanation: The study material explicitly states that list_changed beats an unexpired TTL.

questions.question: Generated code in a sandbox calls tools through the host broker. The user approved running the script once. The implementation then treats that as blanket approval for every tool call the script makes. What is the concern?

options.text: No concern; script approval equals all future tool approvals
Code mode still requires per-call authorization; credentials also remain with the broker
Sandbox code should receive raw OAuth refresh tokens
Code mode requires direct network access

questions.explanation: In code mode, tool calls still follow per-call authorization. Credentials remain with the broker and generated code should not get direct network credentials.
